strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practical problem: existing sparse-attention methods for MLLMs are typically applied post-hoc/training-free and do not actively train the model to be robust to sparsification, limiting achievable inference speedups.

The proposed idea of using GRPO with a joint accuracy + token-reduction reward, sampled across randomized sparsity thresholds, is a simple, low-engineering-overhead way to align training with the inference-time sparse-attention pipeline.
Reasonably broad empirical coverage: 3 base models (Qwen2VL-7B, Qwen2.5VL-3B/7B) and 13 benchmarks spanning both image and video modalities.

Reported results show large token-ratio reductions (from ~70-80% down to ~21-25%) with generally small accuracy degradation relative to both the full-attention model and the ZipVL baseline, suggesting the method is at least directionally effective.
weaknesses: No wall-clock latency, throughput, or memory measurements are reported despite the paper's central motivation being inference-time acceleration; only the abstract 'token ratio' metric is shown, which does not directly demonstrate the claimed efficiency benefits in practice.

No ablation studies are provided: the effect of the KL term, the equal weighting between performance and efficiency rewards, the number of sampled responses N, or the range of thresholds p are all unexamined, making it hard to assess robustness of the design choices.

Only a single operating point on the efficiency-performance tradeoff is reported per model; there is no Pareto curve or analysis showing how ZipR1 behaves across a range of target token budgets, which would better substantiate the 'jointly optimizes the tradeoff' claim.

The only baseline is ZipVL, a training-free method; there is no comparison to other token-pruning/sparse-attention approaches (e.g., FastV, MInference) or other RL-based efficiency-reward schemes, making it hard to gauge the significance of the contribution relative to the broader literature.

Technical novelty is limited: the method largely combines an existing sparse-attention mechanism (ZipVL) with an existing RL algorithm (GRPO) and a straightforward linear combination of two rewards; no new theoretical or algorithmic insight into why this training-time reward encourages more sparsity-robust representations is provided.
Missing implementation and training details (learning rate, number of training steps/epochs, compute/GPU hours, batch size, group size N) which harms reproducibility.

No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported, and some benchmarks (e.g., EgoSchema for Qwen2VL-7B, drops from 66.0 to 64.2) show non-trivial degradation that is not discussed or analyzed.

The paper is very short (essentially 4 pages of content) and lacks a related work/discussion section that meaningfully differentiates the approach from prior sparsity-inducing training methods (MOBA, NSA, structured regularization) mentioned only briefly in the introduction.

No qualitative or quantitative analysis is given for why RL-trained sparsity behaves differently from simply tuning the threshold p of ZipVL directly, which is important to justify that RL training is actually necessary versus simpler alternatives.

strengths: The core idea of directly optimizing the efficiency-performance tradeoff via RL/GRPO, rather than relying on static thresholding of sparse attention, is a reasonable and practically motivated direction for MLLM inference acceleration.

The reported token ratio reductions (from ~70-80% with ZipVL down to ~22-25% with ZipR1) with near-identical accuracy across three model backbones (Qwen2VL-7B, Qwen2.5VL-3B/7B) are numerically impressive if valid.
The evaluation spans a reasonably broad set of 13 image and video benchmarks, suggesting the method is not overfit to a narrow task distribution.
The method is conceptually simple and could be easy to reproduce/build upon given only two reward terms and a standard GRPO formulation.
weaknesses: Missing the single most important baseline: naively running ZipVL (or the constrained optimization in Eq. 3) with a lower p / lower token ratio to match ZipR1's achieved ratio. Without this comparison, it is impossible to tell whether RL training contributes anything beyond simply choosing a more aggressive fixed threshold at inference time.

No ablation isolating the contribution of the KL term, the efficiency reward weighting, the number of sampled responses N, or the range of thresholds used during training/exploration — the reward is a simple unweighted sum (r = r_per + r_eff) with no justification or sensitivity analysis for this design choice.

Despite motivating the work entirely around 'computation and memory bottlenecks' and 'inference-time acceleration,' the paper reports only token ratios and never measures actual wall-clock latency, throughput, or memory/KV-cache footprint, leaving the central efficiency claim empirically unverified.

No comparison to other sparse-attention or token-pruning baselines mentioned in the introduction (e.g., FastV [2], MInference [11], MOBA, NSA), nor to a simpler non-RL distillation baseline (e.g., SFT/KL-only self-distillation on the sparse model without the RL reward), which would test whether GRPO is actually necessary versus simpler alternatives.

The paper reports a single operating point (p=0.975) rather than a Pareto curve across token ratios, so the claimed 'jointly optimized' tradeoff is not actually demonstrated across a range of efficiency levels.

The manuscript is extremely short (4 pages of content) with a thin experimental section, minimal methodological detail (e.g., training hyperparameters, compute budget, number of RL steps/epochs, group size N, how p_n is sampled at training vs. fixed at inference), and no discussion of RL training overhead versus inference-time savings.

Multiple writing/citation issues: 'MOBA and NSA' are mentioned without citation numbers, 'RL-baseed' typo, inconsistent terminology ('well-posed' vs 'well-trained'), and general lack of polish suggesting the paper was submitted in an unfinished state.

No variance/repeated-run reporting; given some reported differences between Full/ZipVL/ZipR1 are within 0.1-0.5 points on several benchmarks, it's unclear whether the reported 'minimal accuracy decline' is statistically meaningful or within noise.

The technical contribution is fairly incremental — applying an existing GRPO recipe with a straightforward reward on top of an existing sparse-attention method (ZipVL) — without new algorithmic insight into why RL is uniquely suited to this problem versus simpler calibration or supervised approaches.

strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: encouraging token sparsity in already sparse-attention-augmented MLLMs via RL, aligning training with the actual inference-time sparse attention process (rather than post-hoc pruning that is inconsistent with deployment).
The proposed reward design (accuracy + token reduction ratio, sampled across random Top-p thresholds) is conceptually simple and easy to implement on top of GRPO.
Reasonably broad empirical evaluation across three base models (Qwen2VL-7B, Qwen2.5VL-3B/7B) and 13 benchmarks spanning both image and video modalities.

Consistent trend across nearly all benchmarks: ZipR1 achieves substantially lower token ratios (from ~70-80% down to ~21-25%) than the ZipVL baseline while largely matching or even slightly exceeding full-attention accuracy in several cases, suggesting the method is not simply trading accuracy for efficiency.
weaknesses: The paper is extremely short (4 pages of content) and lacks depth of analysis: no ablations on reward weighting (equal combination of rper and reff is asserted without justification or ablation), no ablation on the KL coefficient β, number of samples N, or the range of thresholds p, all of which likely strongly affect the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff.

No actual wall-clock latency, throughput, or memory measurements are reported — only the abstract token ratio metric. Since the paper's central claim is about 'inference-time acceleration,' the absence of real speedup numbers (prefill latency, decoding throughput, KV-cache memory) is a significant gap.

No discussion or safeguard against reward hacking: since the efficiency reward directly rewards lower token ratio, there is a risk the policy learns to minimize tokens somewhat independent of comprehension quality; no analysis is given to rule this out (e.g., token ratio vs. difficulty correlation, case studies).

Limited baselines: the only sparse-attention comparison is ZipVL; no comparison to other token pruning/merging methods for MLLMs (e.g., FastV, VisionZip, or other training-based sparsification approaches) that could contextualize how much of the gain is due to RL vs. the underlying Top-p sparse attention itself.
No error bars, variance across seeds, or statistical significance testing, which is especially important given GRPO training can be noisy and sample-efficiency-sensitive.

Reproducibility details are minimal: training hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, GPU/compute budget, number of RL steps, group size N) are not reported, and no code/checkpoint release is mentioned in the main text.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental — it is largely a direct application of GRPO with a two-term reward on top of an existing sparse attention method (ZipVL), without new algorithmic contributions to RL, reward shaping, or sparse attention design.

The related work discussion is very thin (a few sentences in the intro) and does not adequately position the work against the broader token-reduction/KV-cache-compression literature or other RL-based efficiency methods.

Some performance gains (e.g., MMStar, ChartQA in Qwen2VL-7B) exceed the full model's accuracy, which is not discussed or explained — this raises questions about whether the effect is due to noise, evaluation variance, or an actual denoising effect from the KL-based self-distillation, but the paper offers no analysis of this.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated reformulation of token sparsity as an explicit, end-to-end RL objective (via GRPO) rather than a proxy loss or hand-fixed pattern, directly addressing the train/inference mismatch of prior SFT-based sparsification methods.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 13 image/video benchmarks and multiple model families (Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL at two sizes, LLaVA-Video), consistently showing large token-ratio reductions (e.g., ZipVL's ~80% down to ~25%) with minimal accuracy loss.

Strong and fair comparisons against a wide range of relevant baselines, including training-free sparse attention (FastV, VisionZip, ZipVL, Minference) and post-training sparsity-enforcing baselines (MOBA, attention-sharpness regularization), with Sparsity Forcing generally dominating the efficiency-accuracy frontier.

Useful ablations covering different sparse attention mechanisms (top-k/threshold/top-p), budget-range and group-size choices, and a clear rationale for choosing grouped-rollout RL over DPO given the non-stationarity of the optimal budget during training.

Practical, deployment-relevant efficiency measurements (up to 3x memory reduction and 3.3x decoding speedup at long context lengths) plus robustness checks (HallusionBench) and qualitative analysis of learned layer-wise sparsity patterns.
weaknesses: The method is tightly coupled to ZipVL's top-p sparse-attention mechanism as the policy's action space; while the paper claims generality to 'any sparse attention mechanism,' this is only lightly explored (Table 4) and the core reward/exploration design (sweeping threshold p) is specific to nucleus-style sparsification.

Training overhead of the multi-budget rollout scheme is significant (sequential rollouts per query due to different KV-cache trajectories per budget, as the authors admit in Limitations), but no quantitative training-time/compute-cost comparison against baselines or the base RL training itself is provided.

The group-level indicator C used to avoid efficiency bias when no rollout is correct is a reasonable but somewhat ad hoc engineering fix; the paper offers limited theoretical analysis of its effect on the reward landscape beyond the qualitative justification given.

No analysis of training stability/variance across seeds, which is a known concern for GRPO-style RL post-training; a single-run report of final metrics limits confidence in reproducibility of the reported gains.

Model diversity is somewhat narrow (essentially Qwen-VL family plus one LLaVA-Video model); it is unclear how well the approach generalizes to other MLLM architectures or non-Qwen backbones with different attention/KV-cache implementations.

The comparison with trainable sparse attention baselines (MOBA, sharpness loss) is done at a fixed 25% budget while Sparsity Forcing lands at ~26.4%, which is close enough to be fair, but a more systematic sweep of baseline budgets to match various operating points would strengthen the comparison.

strengths: Addresses a practically important limitation of existing sparse-attention methods for MLLMs, which plateau around 50% token reduction; the paper pushes reduction to the 75-80% range while largely preserving accuracy.

Reformulating efficiency (token reduction ratio) and correctness as a joint, end-to-end RL reward (rather than a proxy objective like attention sharpness or a fixed architectural budget) is a reasonable and relatively clean idea, and ties training-time objective to actual inference-time behavior.

Broad empirical coverage: 13 image and video benchmarks, multiple backbone families (Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL at two sizes, LLaVA-Video), and comparisons against several relevant training-free (FastV, VisionZip, ZipVL, Minference) and post-training (MOBA, attention-sharpness regularization) baselines.

Reports concrete systems-level benefits (up to 3x memory reduction, 3.3x decoding speedup) in addition to accuracy numbers, and includes ablations on sparse-attention variants, p-range/group-size, and a hallucination/robustness check on HallusionBench.
weaknesses: A critical ablation is missing: since inference always fixes p at the upper bound (0.975) of the training range, it is unclear how much of the gain comes from the RL/multi-budget exploration versus simply fine-tuning the ZipVL-augmented policy (e.g., with standard SFT/distillation against the reference model's outputs) at a fixed high-p operating point that matches inference. Without this baseline, the paper's central claim that RL and multi-budget rollouts are necessary (as opposed to a much simpler training recipe) is not well substantiated.

The reward design (Eq. 8-9) gates the efficiency term on whether at least one rollout in the group is correct, but the paper provides no empirical analysis of how often this indicator is active during training or how sensitive results are to this design choice, despite claiming it is crucial to avoid efficiency-biased collapse.

Method novelty is incremental: it largely combines GRPO-style group-relative RL (already standard for reasoning tasks) with an existing sparse-attention mechanism (ZipVL's top-p pruning), and the 'any sparse attention mechanism' generality claim is only tested with closely related variants (top-k, threshold, top-p) of the same underlying scheme rather than structurally different mechanisms (e.g., block-sparse MOBA/NSA-style or merging-based VisionZip-style attention).

Training uses only 8 video frames while inference is evaluated with 110-120 frames (16k-20k tokens), a substantial train-test context-length mismatch; the paper does not analyze why/whether the learned sparsity policy generalizes reliably across this large gap beyond a single scaling plot.

Reported accuracy differences between Sparsity Forcing and strong baselines like ZipVL/Full are often within 0.1-0.5 points on several benchmarks, with no reported variance, multiple seeds, or significance testing, making it hard to assess whether the improvements are reliable rather than noise.

The additional training cost of multi-budget sequential rollouts (acknowledged as a limitation) is not quantified (e.g., wall-clock/GPU-hours) relative to baselines, making it difficult to judge the practical cost-benefit trade-off of the proposed post-training procedure.

Some baseline comparisons (e.g., MOBA with a fixed block size of 256 and untuned budget, sharpness-loss regularizer) may not be fully optimized for the MLLM setting, raising fairness concerns about whether the comparison fully reflects the best achievable performance of competing approaches.

strengths: Novel formulation that reframes the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff for MLLM token sparsity as an explicit, on-policy RL objective (GRPO with multi-budget rollouts) rather than a proxy loss (attention sharpness) or a rigid architecture (MOBA/NSA), directly addressing a real mismatch between training and inference-time sparsity.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 13 image/video benchmarks and multiple backbones (Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL at two scales, LLaVA-Video), showing consistent large token-ratio reductions (e.g., ZipVL's ~80% down to ~25%) with minimal accuracy loss.

Good set of ablations: comparison of sparse-attention mechanisms (top-k, threshold, top-p) used within the framework, sensitivity to p-range and group size, and a well-justified design choice for gating the efficiency reward on group-level correctness to avoid degenerate efficiency-only optimization.

Practical, deployment-oriented evaluation including wall-clock decoding speedups (up to 3.3x) and memory savings (up to 3x) against FlashAttention-2, plus a hallucination robustness check (HallusionBench) under low budgets.

Reasonably thorough related-work positioning distinguishing the method from trainable sparse attention (MOBA, NSA) and sharpness-regularization approaches, with a clear articulation of why grouped-rollout RL is preferred over DPO-style preference pairs given the non-stationary optimal-budget target.
weaknesses: The underlying sparse-attention mechanism (top-p pruning) is adopted wholesale from ZipVL; the paper's novelty is largely the RL training recipe layered on top of an existing sparsification method, which somewhat limits the technical contribution.

The paper acknowledges (in Limitations) that multi-budget rollouts must be executed sequentially per threshold p, which likely incurs substantial training overhead versus SFT or standard GRPO training, but no quantitative training cost/GPU-hour comparison is given against baselines, making practicality assessment difficult.

The reward design (gating the efficiency term on whether at least one rollout in the group is correct) is a reasonable heuristic but is only lightly justified/ablated; potential failure modes (e.g., when no correct rollout exists across many consecutive steps, or over-optimistic reward hacking toward specific p ranges) are not deeply analyzed.

Baselines for the 'post-training' comparison (MOBA, sharpness-loss) are adapted in a possibly non-ideal way (MOBA is originally designed to be trained from scratch), and this comparison (Table 3) is conducted on a narrower set of benchmarks (4) than the main results (13), raising some concern about cherry-picking or incomplete validation.

Generalization evidence is somewhat narrow: nearly all experiments use Qwen-family models, with only one LLaVA-Video data point; broader architecture diversity (e.g., other MLLM families or LLM-only long-context settings) would strengthen claims of general applicability.

No variance/repeated-run statistics are reported for benchmark scores, and given some deltas between methods are small (e.g., <1 point), it's hard to assess statistical significance of reported improvements.

The method fixes p=0.975 at inference regardless of training-time multi-budget exploration, which raises the question of whether the RL training's dynamic budget exploration is fully leveraged at deployment or if a simpler fixed-threshold policy could achieve similar results with less training complexity.
